newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian budget running stronger than forecast.
newsitem.headline: Australian budget running stronger than forecast.

text.p: The Australian government's finances were running far ahead of schedule in March, implying a lower 1996/97 deficit than forecast in the mid-year review.
The rolling-12-month budget deficit has fallen from A$10.3 billion in June 1996 to just A$6.2 billion in March -- already better than the A$8.5 billion forecast for June 1997.
To meet the official forecast, fiscal performance in the final three months of the current fiscal year will have to be substantially worse than the same period last year.
(See table below.)
Allowing for a few known distortions, the current trajectory of revenue will exceed forecasts by about A$1.3 billion while spending undershoots by A$1.4 billion.
If that happened, the 1996/97 underlying budget deficit would be just A$5.8 billion.

Even on conservative assumptions the deficit would come in at around A$7 billion. Those conservative assumptions are: a retreat in company tax performance to match forecasts, and other net fiscal flows in the final quarter no better than last year.
At the very least, the budget appears far more likely to produce a deficit lower than expected, rather than higher.
There are reasons for caution, however. Some expenditure sectors are running implausibly below target, suggesting a burst of spending in the final three months of the fiscal year.
Analysis of the budget -- using a rolling 12-month methodology checked with fiscal analysts -- reveals:
REVENUE
Individuals income tax, including pay-as-you-earn, is running close to target. That is, its current trajectory will take it close to the official forecasts for the year to June.
Other forms of income tax are well ahead of schedule, by as much as A$1 billion if one allows for a big bring-forward in company tax and cash from a legal dispute over resource rent.
Other forms of tax are close to target.
But interest and dividends may be stronger than forecast.
EXPENDITURE
On the spending side there are many offsetting ups and downs.
Education spending is well ahead of schedule. Its current trajectory will exceed the full-year forecast by A$700 million.
So far, however, spending for the sector is little changed from previous years, implying an A$800 million undershoot.

A line in the communications budget called "repayment of advances" shows a much smaller allowance for receipts (which are counted on the expenditure side of the budget as unspending) for 1996/97 than 1995/96, and this may partly explain the situation.

But defence spending is on track to undershoot its budget by about A$350 million. Since the Defence Department does not normally underspend by that much, a burst of spending will presumably consume the allocation as June 30 approaches.
Social security, however, is heading towards fiscal-year spending A$200 million or A$300 million below budget, and there is no evident reason why things should change in April, May and June.
The biggest mystery on the spending side is tranport and communications, the 1996/97 budget for which was doubled to A$1.7 billion.
